titel: Leviathan (1651), Introduction and Part I, ch. I–V
claim: Reason is “nothing but Reckoning” — the founding sentence of the computational theory of mind, together with the Introduction's artificial animal and artificial man.
geplant: De Corpore, Part I (“Computatio sive Logica”), from the 1656 English Elements of Philosophy.

titel: Anthology: Monadology · binary arithmetic · characteristica · ars combinatoria
sprachen: French · Latin · English (Latta 1898 PD + working translations)
claim: The program of a universal symbolic language and a calculus of reasoning (“Calculemus!”), binary arithmetic — and, in Monadology §17, the mill argument: the first great objection to machine minds.

titel: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought (1854), Preface, ch. I–III and XXII
claim: The laws of thought written as algebra: logic becomes calculation, and calculation becomes — three generations later, through Shannon — circuitry.
geplant: The Mathematical Analysis of Logic (1847), introduction.

titel: Begriffsschrift (preface), Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik (selections), Über Sinn und Bedeutung (complete)
claim: The formal system itself: quantified logic (1879), and the sense/reference distinction (1892) on which knowledge representation and formal semantics still stand.

titel: The flying man: al-Ishārāt wa-l-tanbīhāt, Namaṭ III, opening (c. 1030)
claim: The oldest counter-voice: a man created complete but suspended in open air — sight void, limb not touching limb — would still affirm his own existence. Self-awareness owes nothing to organ, intermediary, or act: the consciousness objection, six centuries before Descartes and Leibniz's mill.

titel: Discours de la méthode (1637), Part V
claim: The two tests that no machine could pass — language used “to reply appropriately to everything said in its presence”, and general reason: the Turing test, stated in the negative, three centuries early.

titel: L'Homme Machine / Man a Machine (1747)
claim: The radical answer to Descartes: man does not merely resemble a machine — he is one. Materialism about mind, a century before Darwin, two before McCulloch and Pitts.

titel: Maelzel's Chess-Player (1836), complete
claim: The hoax as thought experiment: the Turk must conceal a mind, Poe argues, because chess — unlike Babbage's engine, whose steps are “fixed and determinate” — admits no certain progression: where calculation ends, judgment begins. Carried here is not the automaton but the debate about mechanized thought that a fraud forced into the open.

titel: Notes on Menabrea's Sketch of the Analytical Engine (1843)
claim: Note G: the Analytical Engine “has no pretensions whatever to originate any thing” — the Lovelace objection, which Turing answered by name in 1950 and which the generative-AI debate re-argues today.

titel: On the Mechanical Performance of Logical Inference (1870), selections
claim: The first machine that actually drew logical conclusions — Boole's algebra cast in wood and brass, and a sober early assessment of what mechanized reasoning can and cannot do.

titel: Logical Machines (1887), complete
claim: A working logician reviews the reasoning machines of his day and asks precisely our question: what part of thought is mechanical, and what part is not.

titel: Pensées — five fragments on machine and thought
claim: “The arithmetical machine produces effects which approach nearer to thought than all the actions of animals” — with the immediate rider: but it does nothing from will.

titel: Darwin among the Machines (1863) · The Book of the Machines (Erewhon, ch. XXIII–XXV)
claim: Evolution applied to the machines, four years after the Origin of Species: machines as a nascent 'mechanical life' whose consciousness may yet supervene, man as their reproductive organ — and, in Erewhon, a civilization that abolishes its machines in self-defence. The root of every later machine-evolution argument.

titel: Grundlinien einer Philosophie der Technik (1877), selections
claim: The projection reversed: man is no machine — the machine is an unconscious projection of his organs, and technology the organ of his self-knowledge. The founding text of the philosophy of technology, whose telegraph/nervous-system chapter prefigures the brain/computer analogy.

titel: Ars brevis (1308) — prologue, alphabet and figures
claim: The deepest root: combinatorial wheels that generate propositions mechanically — the art Leibniz named as the inspiration of his ars combinatoria.

titel: Ars magna sciendi, sive combinatoria (1669), selections
claim: The Baroque revival of Llull's art, midway to Leibniz: a universal combinatorial method built on nine principles, tested against Lull as against a touchstone — and pushed to its own limit, where 36 terms yield propositions no ocean of ink could write down. The generative explosion, stated and feared, a generation before the ars combinatoria.

titel: The Algebra (c. 820), the author's preface and opening
claim: The name behind the word: from al-Khwārizmī — Latinized Algoritmi — came algorithm, from his al-jabr came algebra. His preface states the ethos of cumulative science; his opening reduces all calculation to number, and number to units.

titel: The zāʾirja: letter-machine and its critique (Muqaddima, 1377)
claim: The letter-combinatorial answering machine of the medieval Maghrib — the Arabic counterpart of Llull's wheels — described, defended against the charge of fraud, and epistemically dismantled: its answers are well-formed and question-conforming, and coherence of discourse is no proof of conformity with reality.

titel: The trigrams and the binary: two passages of the Great Commentary
claim: One, two, four, eight: the doubling generation of the trigrams that Leibniz — shown the hexagrams in Bouvet's letters from Beijing — read as his own binary arithmetic anticipated. The corpus's Leibniz module cites “Fohy” by name; here is what he saw.

titel: The automaton of Yan Shi (Liezi V, Tang wen)
claim: The oldest complete automaton narrative: the artificer's man-machine sings, postures — and winks at the king's concubines; disassembled, it is leather, wood, glue and paint. Remove the heart and speech fails: the inspection of Leibniz's mill, told two millennia earlier.

titel: The self-working tools: Iliad XVIII · Politics I 4
claim: Hephaestus' tripods go αὐτόματοι to the assembly of the gods, his golden handmaids have mind, voice and strength — and Aristotle draws the conclusion: tools that obeyed or anticipated command would need no servants and no slaves. The argument from automation, stated once and for all.

titel: The golem: Tanach · Talmud · Sefer Yetzirah · Grimm (1808)
claim: Creation by letters, unmasked by silence: Rava's created man is sent back to dust because he cannot answer speech — the language test as narrative, a millennium before Descartes — and one effaced letter turns truth (emet) into death (met).

titel: Der Zauberlehrling (1797/98), complete
claim: The runaway command: an animated servant that executes literally, a countermeasure that doubles it, and the forgotten stop-word — «Die ich rief die Geister / Werd ich nun nicht los». Wiener made it the emblem of the control problem.

titel: R.U.R. — Rossum's Universal Robots (1920), selections
claim: The threshold: in Prague, where the golem legend had settled, the made servant of myth becomes the manufactured worker — «he threw out the man and made the Robot» — and the word robot enters every language.

autor: The brazen head — legend and critic
titel: The brazen head: The Famous Historie of Fryer Bacon (1627) · Naudé, Apologie (1625)
claim: «Time is. Time was. Time is past.» — the speaking brass head that Bacon and Bungay make, and lose to a servant's inattention; set beside Gabriel Naudé's cool dismantling of the same legend told of Albert the Great, the «Androide» broken by Aquinas. The tale and its debunker together — for the head never was.
